newsitem.title: UK: Ready to wear Margaret Thatcher mantle?.
newsitem.headline: Ready to wear Margaret Thatcher mantle?.

text.p: Britain's Defence Minister Michael Portillo posed proudly by a Challenger tank with British troops in Bosnia, flying the flag for NATO in the Balkans.

But does the one-time acolyte of former British leader Margaret Thatcher have the firepower to challenge for leadership of the Conservative Party if Prime Minister John Major resigns after this year's election?
"Politics is one step at a time and it is also (an up and down game of) snakes and ladders," is all the darling of party right-wingers will say when probed about his fierce ambition.
Gone are the days when the flamboyant Portillo would launch into jingoistic tirades, saying British troops would refuse to die for Brussels in a pan-European army.
Gone is the coded sniping at Major over Europe and the barely concealed signals about the prime minister not being robust enough against creeping European federalism.
The Portillo of today is the soul of discretion, a picture of loyalty. This is a canny politician who at the age of 43 appears to be playing a waiting game.
He resisted the temptation to throw his hat into the ring when fellow right-winger John Redwood challenged Major for the party leadership. He may not be so reticent next time.
AMBITION "TO DO WHAT I DO WELL"
The minister who inspires strong passions plays his cards close to his chest.

"I don't think I would be defence secretary today if I hadn't been ambitious," he confessed after a recent morale-boosting visit to British troops serving with NATO's Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia.
"But my ambition is to do what I do well. And if I do, then something else may happen," he told reporters when pressed about his long-term ambitions.
With his deep voice, latin looks and swept-back hair, Portillo is a powerful magnet to Conservative party ladies of a "certain age."
But the satirical magazine Private Eye said he has "the eyes of an assassin and the lips of a tyrant."
Columnist Andrew Rawnsley said: "I suspect he protests his patriotism so ridiculously because he fears others question it."
Julie Burchill in the Sunday Times said: "I don't approve of Portillo. Nobody with half a heart approves of him."
But she added: "He affects us in the same way Thatcher did -- the sheer relief of having a fanatic in charge who doesn't lie to you."
EXOTIC BACKGROUND FASCINATES
Portillo's exotic background fascinates the media. His refusal to do profile interviews fuels the mystique.
He is the son of a Scottish mother and a Spanish Republican father who fled Spain to avoid having to fight friends and relatives in the Civil War.
He was a child star as The Ribena Kid, featured in adverts for a blackcurrant fruit drink.

After a year in business, he joined Conservative Party headquarters. In 1979, he was assigned to give daily briefings to Thatcher in the run-up to the general election that launched her Conservative reign.
She was his political inspiration and the "Iron Lady" carefully nurtured her ideological protege.
He joined the House of Commons as a member of parliament in 1984. After succeeding Thatcher, Major made Portillo the youngest member of the cabinet in 1992 by appointing him a Treasury minister.
Next followed a stint as employment secretary before he was appointed to the defence portfolio that he clearly revels in.
The man who once fought to cut the defence budget when he was at the Treasury now backs the armed forces to the hilt. Officers admire his intellect and command of complex briefs.
A VERY PRIVATE POLITICIAN
But Portillo refuses to pander to a personality cult.

However hard reporters chisel away at the smooth exterior, little can be chipped away from this very private politician who could be one of the frontrunners should a leadership battle develop if Major loses the election in the coming months.

Few chinks can be glimpsed in his armour. "I have avoided doing profile pieces because you are asked questions which lead you to give answers that look stupid," he confessed to reporters who travelled with him to Bosnia.
"People also believe that if you are in a profile, you are promoting yourself," he argued.
The opposition Labour Party are opinion poll favourites to end almost two decades in the political wilderness and win the general election that must be called by May.
The future of the Conservatives could then become a high- risk poker game with Portillo not showing his hand until the very last moment.

For now he remains mandarin-like in his inscrutability, determined to press on at defence and insisting: "If you do too much to distract people from what you are actually doing, it leads them to believe you cannot be doing that job very well."
